speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take too much of the committee's time in order to deal with labour conditions on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Labour. I mentioned the matter briefly during the budget debate, but I want to recall certain points and, more particularly, to make a few suggestions to the government.
I have pointed out before in this house, that labour conditions in the riding of Lapointe and throughout the Saguenay-Lake St. John area, are on the whole pitiful. Just about one family head out of four is without a job and, considering that next week, that is in mid-May, supplementary benefits paid out to the jobless will come to an end, I think this is a very deplorable situation, urgently in need of attention. It is all right to help the unemployed so that their wives and children may eat, but I am of the opinion that this is a short-sighted solution from those who are responsible for administrating this country's business.
As I said, there are in my constituency of Lapointe, and in the neighbouring area about 17,000 people-fathers or heads of families-who will be out of work and most of whom will no longer receive supplementary unemployment insurance benefits. Among the many people affected by

unemployment in my area, there are a good many young men, and to me, this is one of the most tragic situations that can exist.
Unemployment can foster all the seamiest aspects of society. Young people of 17, 18, 20, 25 or even 30 years, who have no work can engage in any adventure, even in crime, because of the despondency they feel when they find that, as they have no work, they cannot help their family to subsist and to eat when they are hungry.
I am aware of such cases as are, I am sure, many of my colleagues.
During the Easter holidays-I am not setting myself as an example, I am merely stating a fact, and I am sure many of my colleagues have had the same experience- I had to send out several hampers of food- paid out of my allowance, since I have no other source of income-to families whose fathers and older children were out of work, even after they had desperately tried to find jobs. I called on those families; I did not content myself with receiving the heads of families at home to give them money directly; on the contrary, I rented cars and paid them a visit, thus seeing with my own eyes that there was hardship in many families of my constituency. I am of the opinion that this is the problem that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) should try to solve for next fall and next winter.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to quote from the words of His Eminence Cardinal Leger, but before I do so, I should like to make a statement. There are many politicians who like to quote church authorities or hobnob with the clergy, in order to gain more prestige with their constituents. I should like to state here, and very categorically, that I am not quoting His Eminence Cardinal Leger, merely because he is the highest Catholic church authority in the province of Quebec. I do so, because he wrote a letter about unemployment which, in my opinion, is a genuine charter from which the federal government could derive inspiration in its search for a solution to the evils from which we are suffering today, and to those which threaten us in the future.
Concerning unemployment, here is what His Eminence Cardinal Leger said:
It has been stated by an economist that, if a man suffers from unemployment for an extended period of time, morbid reactions will almost certainly affect his quality as a man and as a worker. Not only will his technical ability be impaired through disuse but he will lose the habit
Supply-Labour
of working, with consequent loss of self respect and self confidence. So when an opportunity later arises, this man, who previously was merely "unemployed", will have become "unemployable". Meanwhile, his private life may have been shattered, and the atmosphere in which his children grow may have been poisoned.
Though full employment theories remain a subject of discussion among economists, unemployment is no longer considered a natural necessity.
Unemployment places the social order in serious jeopardy, because it can foster, among the unemployed, feelings of discontent and bitterness towards a society which has proved incapable of making use of vital forces crying for an outlet.
The experience of foreign countries tends to prove-
And I want to draw the attention of the government and of the Minister of Labour to that last sentence-
The experience of foreign countries tends to prove that agitators and demagogues always find there a choice field to promote class struggle. Because of the lack of stability from which it rises, unemployment becomes one of the great scourges of mankind.
While impoverishing its victims, unemployment decreases consumption, leads to economic stagnation in other branches of the economy, and paralyses progress. Not only does society not benefit from the development of resources, which are thus truly sterilized, but it has moreover to meet the needs of the unemployed.
The situation has become so serious, as I was saying a few days ago in this house, that throughout the province-and I thought it was only happening in my riding-young people are forming groups in order to rouse public opinion and appeal to the leaders of this country.
I have here an excerpt from La Presse of March 24, 1959, which is preceded by the following headline:
In a pool room, young men are forming an association of jobless.
We also have in my riding such groups of young unemployed men, as well as in the three other ridings of my area.
Mr. Chairman, there is no need to quote statistics, because I know that the Minister of Labour and all hon. members can see, through those statistics, the plight of those who are unable to earn their living and provide for their families. That is why I ask the Minister of Labour to think not only of unemployment insurance benefits, but to try and find some formula to alleviate the terrible scourge which affects not only my own riding, my area and my province, but the country as a whole. There has been some progress I admit, but the situation is still intolerable and the government must do more.
In a letter about unemployment-and I shall come back on this later-His Eminence Cardinal Leger spoke of the responsibility of our leaders with regard to unemployment. I want to quote a passage on page 2897 of that pastoral letter entitled:

Supply-Labour
Those chiefly responsible
Social justice asks all those who are responsible for our economy to create general economic conditions in which it will be possible and easy to exercise the natural right to work. Leadership and economic responsibility are divided among individuals, professional groups and the state. Each must intervene in his own way according to the function he assumes within the economic system.
In our economic system, the responsibility for maintaining existing jobs and for creating new ones rests chiefly with employers and their professional associations.
But the public weal requires much more urgently than in the past that the state intervene in "the division and the distribution of work". Thus, the state in this regard must take new and daring steps, while respecting what Pope Pius XI called "the suppletory function of the state". It must encourage intermediate organizations to take the necessary steps; it must facilitate their action and, if necessary, remedy their deficiencies.
I believe that, in this regard, the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefen-baker) said something that came close to the statement of Cardinal Leger about the economic field; but the Prime Minister of Canada has the means at his disposal and can take the necessary steps to carry out what he has advocated.
I have here a clipping from La Presse of July 9, 1958-that is during the visit of the President of the United States to the parliament of Canada-where I find these words from the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada:
"I believe that the nations of the free world, now united for defence, must, on a world basis, initiate in the field of economy, a new and bold policy designed to ensure prosperity everywhere. It is urgently needed. The communist forces will not wait. Time is against us".
The Prime Minister of Canada understands the problem quite well-I know that, on account of that quotation-and he, more than anyone else in this country, can put in concrete form the ideas he put forward at the time of the United States President's visit. He has colleagues with whom he can discuss the matter. I know it cannot be settled overnight, by why, for instance, a commission could not be set up which would be composed of employers, labour representatives and representatives of certain well-known public organizations, whose devotion to the national common interests is well known? Why could not the government set up such a commission? I am not suggesting anything new to the government, since my leader, the hon. member for Algoma-East (Mr. Pearson) proposed the setting up of such a commission during the 1958 election campaign. That commission could, with the help of both employers and especially workers

study the effects, in several fields of automation in our industry. It could, after such a study, make recommendations to the government which could bring about, over a period of time, concrete results which, each fall and each spring, would save us from the evil of unemployment which affects so many Canadians and so many Canadian families.
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to take more of the time of the house, but I do want to ask the Minister of Labour to consider that matter. I agree he has no time to consider it himself, but why-and I emphasize this point-does not the government think of setting up a commission to consider that problem? It has set up similar commissions in several other fields. It is setting up, for instance, commissions to avoid certain subjects being discussed here in the house. Why not set up a commission to consider the means that could rid us of that spectre of unemployment which afflicts us each fall? That suggestion is not my own, but it seems that next fall and next winter, the unemployment situation will be very serious in Canada, because by next fall many people out of work at present will not be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to close my remarks by quoting again a suggestion made by His Eminence Cardinal Leger, in his letter on unemployment:
We hope that the unemployment problem, as well as so many other urgent matters today, will bring the opportunity of proving by concrete action that overriding community of interests. Would it not be advisable that such a solidarity, which must unite all factors of economic life, take shape through the setting up of joint commissions, grouping labour and employer leaders, in an undertaking of common study and concerted action? Such organizations could also seek efficient means of alleviating the present crisis, of offering concrete plans and obtaining from the state the support and the services deemed necessary. Only such an initiative of employer-labour co-operation, taken in a spirit of co-responsibility with the state, could protect our economic life from the abuses created by either unlimited liberalism leading to anarchy, or by oppressive state control.
Mr. Chairman, may I point out in closing that I have not quoted the words of His Eminence Cardinal Leger in an attempt to cover myself with the cloak of religion, or to try to give more weight, as it were, to the words and suggestions I have offered to the government. I have read this letter from Cardinal Leger at least five or six times, and I think it contains some advice which the government should follow. Here are suggested solutions which would benefit not only the

people of my constituency, or of my area and province, but the whole country, and indeed all the free world.
And let me add this. The other day, the hon. Minister of Labour suggested that Mr. Jean Marchand, who has resigned as labour representative on the unemployment insurance advisory committee, was perhaps a C.C.F. supporter or a Liberal, but was certainly not a member of the Conservative party. I think that has absolutely nothing to do with Jean Marchand's resignation from the unemployment insurance advisory committee. Mr. Chairman, Jean Marchand should be considered only as a representative of labour.

Quite frankly, Mr. Chairman, my union belong to the C.L.C., but I do not know that I am a member of the C.L.C. I said his union is affiliated. These charges have been made continually over the years, yet the people who have the opportunity to do something about it have no intention of doing anything but are glad to make use of him. The Minister of Labour is also aware of another situation, although there have been very few cases in Canada where there has been bad unionism.
This matter also rests pretty well on the doorstep of the government. Last year, or two or three years ago, when the trans-Canada pipe line started crossing northern Ontario we found that the workers who were being hired were already in a union which had a contract already signed. This contract was negotiated between the crown corporation on the one hand and another union on the other, obviously with the government's knowledge and without any objection from them. This is the type of thing which gives unionism a bad name, because it is a sort of backdoor agreement where you sign the contract without having any employees. It means, of course, that the workers themselves have no say in this situation.
But this is always good for news. If there is anything happening which is not happening just the way it is supposed to, then the newspapers play it up. When investigations take place in the United States, although they have no similarity to those in Canada, then we see great big headlines in all the papers. We are not always very helpful to management but I would like to suggest to them that if they continue to do this type of hatchet job on organized labour and do not realize that trade unions are here to stay-they are probably the most democratic organization we have in the country-and if they fail to see the function which a trade union has in industry and in our national affairs as a whole, then they will force those organizations and the various unions into taking other steps to protect the things which they were set up to provide. A union is fundamentally set up to provide its membership with a higher standard of living and to maintain it, to obtain wage increases if they are necessary, to continue to fight for better working conditions, better conditions in the plant and in the community. No union functions only in the plant; all trade unions are publicly minded. More than that, the membership have obtained an education in practical democracy which makes them in many

cases much better fitted for taking their position in the community than many others.
Mr. Chairman, I belonged to the united steelworkers of America in Timmins, and when I was president of the local there we engaged in many things about which I think the country should know but does not normally pay much attention to. We assisted in setting up such things in the community as blood banks. We set them up because there was a need for them, not only for our own members but for all citizens in the community. We supplied the blood to the hospital free on request. We did some of the administration which was necessary to see that this blood was supplied to the needy at a very nominal cost.
We also participated in such things as community betterment, beautifying the town and trying to change the course of a particular creek through the town which had drowned a number of children. In that particular case we did try very hard to get the creek diverted. We were always very interested in civic elections, not only as trade unionists but as individuals. We also took an active interest in the affairs of the community. We helped in addition many welfare organizations, and a lot of trade unionists throughout Canada have headed some of the largest welfare agencies in the country. I think it is safe to say that in Toronto, Windsor and Hamilton they are very proud of the trade unionists who take their places and carry their share of the load in the welfare agencies and in the raising of money for these agencies.
I think these things are too often forgotten. Some fear has been expressed in the last day or two about a third party, the new party, whatever its name might be. I suggest this party will come into being if the trade unions are forced to take action because the need is there. It will not be imposed from the top as has been suggested; it will come from a desire on the part of the worker, because when a worker listens to the budget and legislation he is immediately in politics. Fears have been expressed by people, who in my opinion should be more familiar with the operations of the trade unions than they are. They have been expressed by a number of people who, I suggest, should take a closer look at the operations of their local unions.
I am sure that the hon. member for Cape Breton South would be quite welcome to attend a trade union meeting in his own riding-it would presumably be a meeting of the united mineworkers-and I believe the same would apply to the hon. member for Hamilton South, both of whom discussed
Supply-Labour
trade union operations in a very cursory manner. If the hon. member for Hamilton South would drop in at a meeting of the steelworkers union in Hamilton, I am sure he would learn a great deal about parliamentary procedure and about the democratic working of an organization. I am certain, too, he would find that none of the officials was behaving as a United States citizen or as a citizen of any country outside Canada.
Some concern has quite properly been expressed about the manner of the election of a commissioner to the unemployment insurance commission. The unemployment insurance fund is not as simple in its workings as some people believe it to be. It is not a fund which can be pulled out of a hat to end the recession. It is a fund set up to help cushion the effects of seasonal unemployment, to tide over workers employed in industries which do not operate all the year around. All the workers in Canada contribute toward this fund. In fact, they contribute almost half the money, and a portion of the other half is contributed by management.
Management does not hesitate to tell the workers: this is the amount of money we have to spend as our contribution toward your unemployment insurance fund. This contribution is taken into account in the total wage picture which the companies put forward at negotiations. The companies also include other things such as contributions to medical plans, pensions, where they exist, and benefits of that nature, but unemployment insurance enters directly into the wage picture of all employees. So it adds up to this, that the workers are, in effect, paying nine-tenths of the money which goes into the fund. I suggest that if there was not this contribution coming from the employers, the workers could get its equivalent in the form of wages. Labour has asked, through its democratically elected organizations, for some voice in the appointment of these commissioners, and this was granted in the act. I maintain that more consideration should have been given to the representations which were made on this occasion than was in fact shown. This fund, which is operating for the benefit of Canada as well as of the workers who contribute toward it, should always be managed with the utmost consideration for the representations made by labour with regard to it.
The fact is that in the last two or three years, this fund has had two main objectives. One has been the relief of unemployment- the job it was set up to do-and the other has been its usefulness as a means of stemming the tide of the recession. In my view the fund was never set up for that purpose. The fund should be divided into two parts

Supply-Labour
so that it may be clear in which areas it is functioning, and to the extent that it is being used to carry out part of the government's financial policy, contributions should be made to it from the consolidated revenue.
I think the minister might well take some of the advice which has been offered to him. Fortunately, the Minister of Labour is one who has always sought advice and given it some consideration. I think he could follow his well known pattern of behaviour in the past and give some further consideration to this question of the unemployment insurance commission and the representations which have been made to him with regard to it. Knowing, as I do, the attitudes taken by some of his colleagues, I am surprised that the minister has been able to accomplish what he has with regard to unemployment insurance. The workers will certainly appreciate what he has done, though they will not appreciate having to raise the increased amount of money necessary in order to continue the benefits which they are to receive.

These are the changes which will be made in the unemployment insurance regulations.
We had hoped that the minister would by now have indicated his intention to introduce changes in the federal labour code. We had hoped he would have announced his intention to revise this code. Changes in the code are even more necessary now, in the light of events involving labour in the province of British Columbia, and in Newfoundland than they were some time ago. They are also necessary in view of the situation in Ontario. The other day I was discussing with officials of a union in Toronto some of the problems with which they were faced under the industrial relations act of that province. It was pointed out to me that the labour board by stalling and delaying its decisions was making it almost impossible for a union to function. They told me of a situation which had arisen at a plant where some 33 workers were engaged. A request was made for certification. Six months later the board got around to asking for a vote because one employee had, apparently, objected. When the vote was finally taken, only four people were there, the man who had intervened and three of the union people. This is one of the problems they are facing.
As another example, I recall a strike which took place in a small lumber mill at Field, Ontario. Decertification was applied for and the union, as I think the membership would confirm, was ready to agree that any decision taken would be binding on both parties; if the
IMr. Peters.]
decision went against the union, they were willing to leave that particular plant. The period for entering into negotiations was drawing close, and some decision needed to be taken. Mr. Chairman, that strike was over a few months ago, and only the other day the union concerned received a letter saying that it was hoped in the near future to be able to render a decision on the decertification hearing which had been held six or seven months earlier. These delays cause problems in many of the industries enjoying labour contracts.
I wish to thank the Minister of Labour for the assistance he gave to some of the people in my part of the country. In his diplomatic way he intervened in a serious situation in the gold mining industry. I believe he suggested that it would be a good thing if they sat down and negotiated but I am not sure if he sat in on the negotiations. Shortly after that a settlement was reached in the dispute. A few years ago an identical situation developed involving an eight-month strike resulting in the loss of all concerned of thousands of dollars and the settlement reached at that time was not much better received than was the recent one which the minister assisted in obtaining by intervention.
The minister on a number of occasions has said he is investigating all the aspects of the labour code. This is necessary in Canada. If we are going to have a bill of rights I think we should also have a bill of rights for trade unions.
The situation in Newfoundland was probably more dramatic than that which develops in most cases. The results in British Columbia, as the hon. member for Skeena pointed out, will not be much better and it will be longer before we find out what those results are.
The minister must ensure that Canadian labour is guaranteed certain fundamental freedoms under the labour code. The Newfoundland situation illustrates the need of this. It must be remembered that the international woodworkers of America did not go into the province uninvited. The president of district 2 of the I.W.A. was invited to speak at a convention of a company union in 1956 which he accepted. During the course of the convention a motion was put on the floor recommending that this particular union join forces with the I.W.A. As was the case in some of the constitution mentioned by other hon. members who have spoken, the membership did not have the right to affiliate with I.W.A. at that time.
The loggers themselves invited the president to bring the organization into the province which he did. In 1957 organizational work was started in the bush. Eighty-seven per cent of the loggers in the A.N.D. company signed

up in the I.W.A. They applied for certification under the labour relations board and the government turned them down on a technicality. They re-applied to the board in June 1957. I think hon. members should know that in most provinces a bare majority or a majority of 55 per cent will grant certification automatically. In this instance a vote was ordered and held with 86.4 per cent of the loggers voting. It had to be conducted by referendum, I am told. Committees were set up and there are many union committees in the outports and small communities where the loggers live. The I.W.A. in Newfoundland is democratically constituted, has set up committees and holds conventions of its membership.
The union opened negotiations with the Company after certification but these broke down. They applied for conciliation services but these too, broke down. They then applied for a board. The surprising thing is that this board comprising a representative of management, of labour and an impartial chairman voted unanimously in favour of their being granted a 5 per cent increase over a period of two years. The hours were to be reduced from 60 to 54. The company then refused to negotiate and the strike resulted.
My time is nearly up although I should like to continue.

Mr. Chairman, as I listened to the Minister of Labour present his estimates to the committee yesterday I realized he was not dealing with the basic causes of unemployment at all but with the results and with his work in trying to overcome those results. I want to compliment him because I think he is doing the best he can in the circumstances. If the minister wanted to help eliminate unemployment I should think, however, he would speak to the Prime Minister and ask him to forget about the diversion of trade.
The last time the Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke in Port Colborne he said there had been a great deal of trade switched from United States to England and that more would be switched but he has not made a pronouncement to this effect in this house.
I want to relate a few remarks to unemployment in my area. Hon. members will recall that in December 1957, the government sent a trade mission to England comprising 40 or 50 men. They went over to buy but not to sell. That was at a time when England had almost full employment and Canada had considerable unemployment. It will also be recalled that the mission was headed by Mr. Duncan, chairman of the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario, and that the Prime Minister went to Montreal to wish them bon voyage. He said at
Supply-Labour
that time this mission would reap rich rewards. One of the rich rewards obtained for my district was an increase in unemployment.
Hon. members will recall that before departing with the trade mission Mr. Duncan announced a $10 million order for large turbines, generators or something of that nature. Whatever it was, we were told in this chamber that they had never been made in Canada before. I was informed by an engineer that this was true but also that they had not been made in that size in England before, either. Canadian industry expected to have an opportunity to bid on that order. Canadian subcontractors were working on components for that order but Mr. Duncan's announcement killed it altogether. I am not saying that if it had bid Canadian industry would have got the order but I believe Canadian industry should have had an opportunity to bid. If Canadian industry did nothing else, or if Canadian industry was incapable of building that particular turbine or generator, why did it take 40 or 50 men to go to England to buy it, because we have never heard of anything else that they have bought?
It is true that the mission cost Canadians well over $500,000, and when they came back they gave work to some printers down near Toronto to print the report of that particular mission. If you read the report you will find that it reads something like the social pages in the press, the social register. It deals mostly with the social functions they attended, who entertained them, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce joined them, when he left them and when he joined them again and when he left them again, and so forth.

I feel that business would go ahead with greater confidence and we would have more employment in our country.
Much of the unemployment is due to our fiscal policy. I do not think anybody in Canada will deny that our fiscal policy flows from the greatest of all transactions, namely the conversion loan, with which I do not intend to deal.
I regret to see the unemployment insurance fund depleted by some $250 million last year, and I should like to have the minister comment on the loss of $10 million from that account through the sale of bonds. Then he went on to say that he realized advice is the cheapest of commodities, but he does give this government advice and it is the same advice that has been given by many managers of banks, by managers of trust companies, and so on, over the last two years. These are the two courses he says the government should take:
The first is that the government must give the clearest possible indication that its budgetary deficits are temporary and will be turned into

balance or into surplus when the slack in the economy is taken up, and competing demands threaten to push up prices.
The second is that the government must give evidence that it has an effective plan for dealing with unemployment.
In my view, we need to take a new look at unemployment. The problem is changing in character, and needs re-examination to determine more precisely its composition, its causes and how it can be cured.
Unless the problem is thoroughly understood, serious mistakes in policy could be made . . . there is great danger in the crude idea that it is possible for governments to spend their way out of recession and unemployment.
I might say that when the Minister of Finance presented his baby budget in December, 1957 I expressed this in a somewhat different way. I said at that time that the government had the mental complex of a man who came to my office. He saw the Globe and Mail lying on the table with big headlines across the top giving the net earnings of the Ontario liquor control board for the previous year, which were very considerable, and he said: "I think we will drink ourselves out of debt yet." Quoting further from Mr. Howe:
The threat of inflation cannot be checked by government alone. The government must, however, inspire confidence and give leadership, first by setting its own house in order, and then by establishing rules that it expects every citizen to follow.
He concludes with these words:
I am confident that the battle against inflation can be won if government leadership is forthcoming.
I think government leadership needs to be forthcoming in order to overcome inflation and unemployment. The government has received advice from financial men over the last two years and has not taken that advice. Mr. Howe is a man who had much experience in parliament. He has said that he never intends to enter politics again and I think it would be well if the government would take his advice at this time because it is certainly parallel to the advice given by many other men in the financial field.
It seems to me that the government could do more to get our unemployed re-established. The minister is doing the best he can but I think he might do more. So many of our unemployed have been out of work so long that they have lost heart. The unemployed make periodic trips to the unemployment insurance offices to get their cheques when they can qualify. They look over the list of vacant jobs and when they cannot find one they go home. They come back again the next week or in two weeks' time. They draw unemployment insurance as
Supply-Labour
long as they can and then they drift to the municipal relief rolls. At least, that is true in my area.
It certainly was not difficult for men to qualify for unemployment insurance in the winter of 1957-58. In fact, the government was so solicitous about the unemployed in my area that they wrote letters to people who were retired and on pension telling them to be sure to go their unemployment insurance offices and get their cheques. Of course, these people had votes and the government was attempting to buy votes with money being contributed by people who were working.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF SUPERVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: What a story that is.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speechtext: The government is not so generous today. It has mismanaged the fund so that at the present time they are calling on industry and the workers to contribute to make up the $10 million loss in bonds and the cost of some of these votes.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF SUPERVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Do you really believe that?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF SUPERVISORY COMMITTEE

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF SUPERVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
There is nothing that injures a person's morale more than idleness. After a time people give up and lead rather aimless lives, making no contribution to our society. There are a good many skilled or semi-skilled jobs for which these people could be trained. It seems to me that since we have so many shortages in certain skilled and semi-skilled occupations and have been going to Europe to get such workers we might have a look among the unemployed and see if we cannot train some of these people.
The government certainly could co-operate with the provinces. In my opinion many of these unemployed people are bright and would be industrious. I think they could be trained. In many hospitals at the present time there are shortages of nurses aids and male attendants, and I think we could easily train such people. There is a marked shortage of nurses. I know one hospital that up to two months ago could not open its new addition because nurses and proper personnel to staff the hospital were not available. I think the government might take the lead in co-operation with the provinces so that many girls might train as nurses. Many of them cannot do so on their own resources and I think that the federal and provincial governments should co-operate to this end.
I happen to know of a very young person who was unemployed last year and got into trouble by stealing. This person was sent to the house of correction for one year and while

Supply-Labour
there learned a skill which she has put to very good use since. As a result, she now has a thriving business. It does not seem to me to be a very good thing that this person should have to go to the house of correction to learn something that she wanted to learn before going there.
There are also many young men idle who might be taught different skills such as carpentry, plumbing and a multitude of others. To my mind it is more expensive not to teach them than it is to teach them. Many of these people are bright and industrious and they should be given a chance. I think it would be a very easy matter for the Department of Labour to classify these people. I do not suggest that a costly commission with expensive economists should be set up but I think that the government could come forward with some type of committee that would make recommendations respecting the unemployed.
I do not think that the government is doing anything about older workers. I know that the other day the minister referred to the fact that this is quite a problem. By "older worker" I mean people between 35 and 40 whom industry will not hire because of the various pension plans. During the last campaign I believe the Prime Minister promised -I remember seeing this in the press although I have not the article here-that working men would be able to take their pensions with them. I do know that it has been said by some that this would not be constitutional but I think it would be constitutional if the government would refuse, in whole or in part, to allow industry their right to deduct their contributions toward pension plans for income tax purposes unless industry is willing to grant workers an earlier vesting of pension rights or give them the right to take their pension with them to another job. I imagine that would probably be constitutional because, after all, we would only be dealing with the Income Tax Act.
There are many reasons why I think workers should have earlier vesting of their pension rights. The plant 'where a man is working might close down. A mine might run out of ore. Woods operations might close down. Then there are many medical reasons. For instance, a man working in an industry might develop a chest allergy or skin allergy and while he would not be sick he could not continue working in that particular plant. I think that the government should devise some means by which there would be earlier vesting of pension rights. I think that this would in itself clear up much of the trouble of the older worker in changing jobs.
I think my time is about up. I would say this. I think unemployment is a great social

problem in our country. We are a young country. We have many resources but we do not seem to know how to handle them. I think this government should take the advice that people have been trying to give them in the last two years. I think it is extremely important that we solve our unemployment problem because it would be to our economic advantage.

Prior to that, in a press
release to the Globe and Mail of last Saturday, May 2, the Leader of the Opposition led off with a statement to the effect that labour organizations had been shockingly ignored and he went on to say there had been government bungling in this matter and that the government would have to take full responsibility. I should like to talk about it for a moment or two since the opposition seem to have dropped this subject. I should like to refer to what the hon. member for Essex East said as reported at page 3364 of Hansard when he was detailing what the duties of the unemployment insurance commission are. He said this:
This is a body that is called upon not only to administer, by way of formulation of policy, matters having to do with unemployment insurance, but this commission actually is a trustee of many millions of dollars contributed not only by the employers but by the workers of this country. At one time there was almost a billion dollars in the fund.
To that he could also add that the fund is built by general contributions of the taxpayers of the country and through government contributions as well. The very fact that it is a semi-policy making commission,

that it is an advisory committee to the minister, that it is called upon to advise, in an impartial and unbiased way, the minister as to what action he should take with regard to the operation of the commission and to future legislation with regard to unemployment insurance surely is, as newspapers all across the country have pointed out, a reason why that commission must be non-political and unbiased.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF SUPERVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
With regard to general labour policy, I believe a great deal has been said in the press and by organizations which tends to damn all labour for the sins of a relatively few unions. Out of some 200 unions in the United States only some seven are involved in the present senate investigation. I think it is at only those seven unions that any public censure has been directed. We always play up in the press the strikes and the walkouts but we do not play up the literally hundreds
66968-9-221
Supply-Labour
of settlements which are made every year where management and labour get together and through collective bargaining iron out their differences and come to a decision between the two parties which is fair to both. The whole essence of labour peace is through honest collective bargaining, with recognition by labour of the problems of management and with management recognizing that labour is entitled to a just share in the wealth of this country.
However, there are conditions which arise- and this matter has been laboured in the house previously-where some of these unions, the odd one of them do certain things. In this respect may I say that I am not talking about the I.W.A. The hon. member for Skeena who spoke about the I.W.A. last night and pointed out what a democratically run union it is, has my full agreement. I know the I.W.A. and I know what a good union it is. It is a good tough union but it is a good union. But I have also heard the hon. member for Kootenay West lambaste Mr. Banks of the seafarers international union. I have also committed that error myself because it is an error to go after Mr. Banks. It is not Mr. Banks who is important but it is the conditions which allow a man like Mr. Banks to have the power and control that he has. If Mr. Banks left the country tomorrow, there would be another man with another name, but the policy would still be the same, namely the policy set out by Mr. Banks. Therefore you must get at the root of the problem before any improvement can be made.
In this regard, just in order to give an instance to the house, I should like to refer to a letter which I received. I may say that I have checked on the facts in this case myself. I received a letter from a Vancouver man, namely Mr. A. Gourley, Sr. who told me-and I think all hon. members received copies of this letter-about the record of his son in the S.I.U. I will quote two paragraphs only. They are as follows:
I instance the case of my son, and I invite the fullest investigation by the Department of Labour. My son was a union seaman for 12 years before the
5.1.	U. acquired jurisdiction. My son then joined
5.1.	U. and paid $75 entrance or initiation fee, $4 monthly dues and an assessment of $15 a year. That represents a serious reduction in take-home pay of an ordinary seaman.
Then like a bolt from the blue, my son was charged verbally with non-payment of union dues although he was working for the Union Steamship Company under the check-off system by which union dues are deducted from pay cheques and are sent direct to the union by the employing company. The fact the charge was a manifest lie did not prevent my son's expulsion and deprivation of the benefits for which he had so dearly paid.
The letter goes on to point out that an actual statement had been received from

Supply-Labour
union headquarters indicating that these dues had been paid and I received the check-off book, and the man's ticket showed that the dues had been paid. It is instances like this where a labour leader is given the power to say a man shall work at his profession, his job, his avocation, or whether he shall not. Those conditions can only be changed by labour itself; they cannot be changed by government action. The government cannot police the wrongs of labour; labour must clean its own house.
In this regard I would suggest to the labour movement that they set up what I call a minimum constitution for their unions. That minimum constitution might be a bill of rights for labour unions, and that would set the standard. The minimum standard which I would suggest would be that leadership of the union must be elected democratically and by secret vote; that there must be a secret vote in all cases of strike action, not only for the sake of the men but also for the sake of the leaders so that they would know they really had the men behind them. Even if these two simple changes were made, then the odd rotten union which is rotten only because of the way its constitution is written which gives its leadership overwhelming dictatorial power, would fall by the wayside. I suggest that if that were a condition of recognition by the Canadian Labour Congress, so then should it be a condition of recognition by any government.
Perhaps it would change a few of the methods of working of some of our unions, for example the railroad unions. They are the oldest unions in the country. In many ways they are the sanest of all unions; they have a tradition and integrity behind them. But even when they call a strike they have open ballots which are sent in to their central regional headquarters for counting. Hon. members remember the recent disagreement which was so ably settled by the Minister of Labour between the firemen and the C.N.R. When the decision was made to strike, that decision was made by the chairmen; perhaps a score or so of men across the country. Now that is not right. Secret ballot is the way that this parliament is elected, and it should also be the way in which unions are operated.
With regard to the question of union publication of their financial statements, I have pointed out before that there are large companies operating in Canada which do not publish their statements, and until we can say that all the affairs of business are open to the public, then we cannot in justice ask that the unions do the same. The labour policy of this government is a progressive one.
[Mr. Broomed
It is a policy which has been praised, particularly in the session of 1957, by hon. members in the Liberal party and hon. members in the C.C.F. party, and it has also been praised this session. The Minister of Labour has received much praise, and no members on the opposite side dare attack the minister. They are playing fair on that point; they do give the minister credit for having done a job which I think ranks him with the best ministers of labour this country has ever had. The criticism we have heard, as I have said before, is backfiring, and I do not think the opposition have a very good case on any matter concerning the Department of Labour.
There are two other points I would like to touch on, Mr. Chairman. With regard to the winter works program which has been so successful, I agree that it would be a good thing for the planning to start as soon as possible so that it can get off to a good start next fall. Even in the very short time which was allowed for the plan to get into operation last year it was an outstanding success. I am concerned too about the problem of older workers. A young engineer came to see me. At least, I thought he was a young engineer. He was 35 years of age and he came to me and wanted to know about a particular company, because he felt he could only make one more job change and then that was the end until he retired, because companies just were not hiring men over 35 years of age. Part of the trouble is because of pension plans. Pension plans are needed and are necessary, but they place a disability on workers, professional people and day labourers who wish to change their jobs after a certain stage in life, because it then becomes too expensive for the company which would have hired them to take them in because of the cost to their own pension scheme. If the pension could be vested in the worker so that he might carry it with him and make his own contribution to the pension scheme of the company he would be moving to, I think it would be very worthwhile. We must also accept the fact that a man of 55 or 60 years of age still has a worth-while contribution to make.
Mr. Chairman, as I said before, I rose to speak in this debate for just a few minutes, and I will close my remarks with the same topic I commenced with. The hon. member for Essex East said that this was still an issue. I would like to quote to him part of an editorial from the Toronto Star, which is certainly not a supporter of this party but I think is a fairly vocal supporter of the party to which the hon. member belongs. This is what the main organ of the Liberal party has to say in its issue of May 4 last. It is headed, "No Injustice to Labour".

We find it hard to summon up a sense of outrage at the government's appointment of A. F. MacArthur of Toronto to the unemployment insurance advisory committee over the objections of the Canadian Labour Congress. And why are the Liberals and C.C.F. making noises as if labour civil rights are being trampled, and talking darkly of raising the issue in parliament? What issue?
It makes sense that the Unemployment Insurance Act should require consultation with organized labour about appointees to represent labour on the committee. But no government can abrogate its right of final decision, after the advice is assessed. Advice is one thing, dictation another. Not the Canadan Labour Congress, nor the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, nor anybody else, should be able to dictate appointments to the Canadian government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF SUPERVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a few minutes ago I was stating how a properly organized union would function, and I mentioned some of the considerations which must be given to it. I did that to give the lie to some of the statements made in the newspapers about the dictatorial methods which are sometimes said to be used by unions. I used the example of the international woodworkers of America and the situation they found themselves in in the province of Newfoundland. This is only an example; there are many others. They conducted such things as organizational drives and they obtained a large number of cards. They received support from a large percentage of the workers, which involved both the paying of money and the signing of cards. Then they applied for certification which was granted by the government. They applied for services from the conciliation branch which were supplied. Then they went through a conciliation board, and that is where they justify to the public at large the conditions they are asking for and the requests they are making in their negotiations. In this particular case it resulted in a unanimous decision of the board.
This decision was agreed to by the conciliation board, but it did not have to be accepted by either the union or the company, and in this case it was not accepted by the company. I think everybody is familiar with the road blocks which were set up by the government intervening in this case. They finally passed a law which said that this union was no longer to be allowed to operate in this particular situation.
How different this is from the justification which must be made by the companies when they wish to obtain an increase in the price of their products. They do not go to anybody and ask permission. They just raise the price, and because of the monopoly control which is evident in a large number of industries, and high prices result. In this particular case as in many other cases some of the road blocks which were put in the way of the 66968-9-221J
Supply-Labour
union involved a hostile government, a hostile board when certification was applied for, and a vote taken under adverse conditions. And then there was what took place after the strike began, when heavy fines were imposed for obstruction and jail sentences were imposed on people for taking part in picket lines and using moral persuasion to prevent other people from stealing their jobs.
I think the complicated operations which the union was willing to go through was a good example of how unionism works in Canada. We hear talk about the right to work, what is meant is the right to "scab" and take somebody else's job, also, in this case, the right of a government to set up an alternative union which is under government control. These are the things that the newspapers should be talking about.
This has been no credit to government, and it should be pointed out that the federal government itself cannot guarantee to all the workers in Canada the right to organize, negotiate and bargain in good faith in any of the provinces in Canada. In this particular instance the board of public opinion was given the facts. For instance, in the mill, the wage rate is not $1.05 an hour; it has been increased to something like $1.78 an hour. At the same time, a wage increase was paid to those mill-workers of between five cents and seven cents an hour, when the basic rate was $1.75. It was also established that this company was not paying the taxes which other companies were paying. The union had to establish in its public relations work before the country in general, that conditions were as they had stated them to be in their negotiations. They not only had to justify themselves to the government, but justify themselves before an impartial board and then, through the board of public opinion, to the country also.
All these things have been done, and yet the rights which a union can normally expect -the rights which a bill of rights would guarantee to all citizens-have been denied in this particular case. There has certainly been an oversight in our federal labour legislation when we cannot, as the hon. member for Vancouver South has just said, have at least a minimum federal labour code to guarantee certain basic rights.
Unions continue to be willing to express their democratic point of view. For years one particular union in which I have been interested, one that is not in the Canadian Labour Congress, has been accused on many occasions of not fighting for the workers whom it represents. Nevertheless, those workers have continually over the years supported that union. Only recently, within the last year, a strike took place in that union. It fought a bitter strike with defection inside its own ranks,

Supply-Labour
even between worker and fellow worker, but it came out with a settlement. Those Unionists were unsatisfied with the leadership they had received, and they did throw out the majority of that leadership and establish a completely new executive. But what help are they getting now from the people who always said: "Let us get rid of the commies who are in this particular union."? What assistance do they get? The other day, one of the staff representatives who has been accused of supporting the old guard in Sudbury was fired because the new executive had put in an auditor and the books were being audited to find out exactly what had happened during past years. This particular staff representative was burning and destroying certain documents, and he was fired. Well, the newspapers, this democratic organization which stands for fine sentiments, did nothing to help the workers who had already made a decision, democratically reached, and who had decided to do something about the position which had been rumoured for a long time. No, the newspapers came out with an article condemning the union for having fired this staff representative, instead of saying: "Let us get to the bottom of this and find out what the situation is."
I remember, also the work done by the newspapers over the years in other areas. In the mining area in Timmins, when I was a miner, we decided we would change unions and bring in the Canadian Congress of Labour so that they should be our bargaining agents. We set up an organizing committee and democratically did the work necessary to bring in these unions, applying for certification and so on. Then we transferred to the steelworkers and we negotiated with the gold mining industry. But we got no help from newspapers which had previously said the unions to which we belonged had been communist dominated. Did we get assistance in setting up better working conditions? I should say not. They immediately changed their tactics and said: the poor industry is in such bad shape that it does not matter who has got control of the unions or what the unions are; there is going to be no assistance. Did the newspapers give any consideration to the other work the unions do in the community? These newspapers have always been on the other side of the fence, and no matter whether a union was under a democratic or any other kind of administration they were more favourable to the industry than they were to the union.
I think the unions over the years have done a great deal of good, and one of the things the minister could do on behalf of organized labour is to draw attention to the

story of how the unions work and are supposed to function. I would not be opposed to the minister developing a minimum constitution for these unions, and I think that if he examines the constitutions of the major unions he will find they are much further advanced than the constitution he would consider to be the minimum.
If the workers wish to change their union, they have that right. When they do not have that right it is being run by people we do not want in this country. Usually the worker has not too much control over that. The only time a union has been at fault or has been guilty of being undemocratic has been when some of the union and company officials co-operate among themselves to sign backdoor agreements or agreements under which money is exchanged under the table and where the union membership has no say in the matter or is not taking an active part. I know of only one or two cases where this has taken place. These cases have been the subject of extended investigation, reams of reports and page after page of newspaper comment. These instances are given much publicity but nothing is said about the thousands of unions that function properly and fairly.
We sometimes hear reference made to the right to work clause. This sounds very good, Most of us would agree that there should be a right to work clause but the right we mean is the right to obtain a job and have full employment. Thousands of people have been unable to enjoy that right this year. This is not the right that would be given under the proposed law in the United States. It would mean that an employer could engage cheap labour working long hours with low pay and few benefits. The dog-eat-dog attitude would prevail and there would be bickering back and forth. There can be no harmony in industry or in labour affairs if a situation of that kind exists.
We have a working force of five million people in Canada and approximately half a million people are now looking for work. If there were no unions today and no contracts and labour legislation as we know them people would be underbidding each other for jobs and a man who lost his employment would offer to go back to work for five cents less. This would lead to a chaotic situation. I do not think anyone in Canada wants that. I do not believe this is what is wanted even by those in industry who are opposed to labour unions. I have heard it said on many occasions in the past by people engaged in management that they are quite satisfied with the unions they have and they have expressed a willingness to continue to increase the

union security. They have expressed appreciation of the co-operation and assistance that only a union can give.
1 should like to mention only one illustration. A few years ago I had the honour of organizing a plant in Kirkland Lake in one of the few industries in that area that is not connected with the gold mining industry. The latter industry has been one of the last strongholds of anti-labour and as far as I know there is no union security in the whole industry. This little plant was organized in a town that is engaged in the gold mining industry. The management of that plant promised that the union security would be increased if the union functioned satisfactorily and lived up to the agreement. It has been increased and there is now a union shop. This happens to be an I.W.A. local. The management was so happy that it negotiated a profit-sharing program. We are very surprised to find that the program is paying more money to the employees now than we would have got under our original negotiations which amount the company said would bankrupt the firm. Management and labour enjoy a good relationship there and management is happy to tell any segment of the industry about their happy experience with the trade union.
This experience has been repeated across the country. The only place where differences of opinion arise is around the bargaining table but this is to be expected because the union is pledged and has the responsibility of getting as much for its employees as it possibly can get. Management on the other hand has the responsibility of getting for the shareholders as much as it can get. One way they can get extra money is through low-priced labour. Both management and labour have an obligation and as the hon. member for Skeena pointed out so clearly this morning they share the obligation to sit down and negotiate in good faith. When contracts are allowed to drag along for a year or two inharmonious labour relations result. Many things build up over the period of time that should never enter into the negotiations. We should endeavour to cut down the length of time that is necessary following an application for conciliation services and the length of time in which a board may sit and bring in its report. Limits must also be imposed when a union goes on strike or when a company locks out the workers from the plant. These limits should be definitely expressed and rigidly adhered to in order to eliminate much of the strife that has been experienced.
I have been interested in the comments of those hon. members representing western
Supply-Labour
constituencies who have participated in this debate. They have been educated through weekly and monthly farm newspapers to think that all farm problems are caused by labour. They should demand that the minister conduct an investigation into this allegation. It is true that a part of the price of an automobile is represented by labour costs and we should know this. I am informed, however, that labour costs represent a total of $300 of the price of a $3,000 car. As the Financial Post pointed out last year the production cost in assembling an automobile is $57. We should know these things. If these facts were brought out by the Department of Labour I do not think the farmers would object. I know they would not be opposed to an automobile worker receiving $300, figuratively speaking, of the cost of a $3,000 car when the manufacturer, dealer and distributor each receive $600.

speechtext: Are you suggesting that the worker who has no investment except the labour he has to offer should share equally with the manufacturer, dealer and distributor and others who invest large sums of money?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF SUPERVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I certainly suggest that the worker should not receive just one-half of what is received by the distributor, dealer and manufacturer. This raises another point. The worker has a big investment in the industry in which he is engaged. A worker may invest his lifetime in a plant. The value of the investment of his working life cannot be estimated in dollars and cents. In many plants the worker does not enjoy pension plan benefits which are, as it were, depreciation. The manufacturer and dealer are allowed depreciation for their equipment. The only one not allowed depreciation by law is the poor worker. The minister should give urgent attention to the question of the establishment of a national portable pension program. This is something that consideration must be given to, because the matter has been raised so often. Everybody else who has an investment is permitted to state what the investment is and to depreciate it but the poor workers who work in those plants are not given the same right.
A good example is that of the international woodworkers in Newfoundland. Those loggers are working in the bush and they are investing in an industry which is returning to them only $1.05, $1.06 or $1.07, or whatever the company has decided to pay since they

Supply-Labour
formed Joey's new union. They are investing their lives in that particular industry and there is no pension plan for them. They are not allowed any depreciation on their income tax for the lifetime that they are spending there nor for the years of seniority they have established. By law we shall have to establish a national portable labour pension plan which will take into consideration the work that a worker does during his lifetime. He invests in the same way as a man who is setting up a factory. He invests in that plant a certain amount of his life and he should be compensated to some extent by having a pension plan which he can carry with him from job to job and from plant to plant. In other words, the Newfoundland workman could carry his pension into the logging industry, into the fishing industry, or into any other plant or allied industry he may be in so that when he spent 20 years of his life working he would have established a pension plan that would give him some consideration for the work he has done.
I do not think the farmers-I am sure this is true-in western Canada or in any place else will disagree that the worker has some rights in a particular plant and that he should be given some consideration. I am quite sure they will not be too concerned because they know it is the workers who buy their agricultural products; it is the workers who keep them on the farm; it is the workers who supply them with the market for their products. They know that the manufacturer eats only the same amount of food as a worker; he eats the same number of eggs as a worker will eat. Because the workers are more numerous, the farmers are much more concerned and should be much more concerned with the workers than with other various aspects of industry. I would strongly urge that when the minister is considering a national labour code he consider putting in something that will give protection in a bill of right for labour, as the hon. member for Vancouver South mentioned, and that he will also give consideration to and be much more willing to recommend the disallowance of legislation in the provincial field that eliminates the rights to which labour is entitled. The minister could give consideration to other matters also.
I should like to refer to one case which comes under the field of the Department of Labour. I refer to the uranium industry. In this instance the workers have not the right to join a second union if they wish. They have not the alternative they wish. Staff representatives of one union are not allowed to go on company property, are not allowed

to visit the bunkhouses of this particular company because the company says this will create some difficulty. It should be pointed out that this union has been in the forefront of organized labour for some time. Consideration should be given to seeing what can be done to allow those workers who may wish to make a change the opportunity of talking to the representatives in their own domicile, which happens to be the company bunkhouses. They should be given this consideration so that they can make a democratic choice for themselves and decide whether they wish to belong to the union of which they are now members or if they wish to change. This would apply also to the other plants and to the other bunkhouses in the area.
I think that workers should also be given the right, when they wish, to join the steelworkers union. They should be given the right to do what they wish. If they wish to join the mine, mill and smelter workers union they should have that right. They should have the free choice to join that union if they wish, and this right should be insisted upon by the Department of Labour.
We have been very concerned also with the fact that the federal Department of Labour has farmed out some of its responsibilities to provincial governments. The instance in Blind River is a good example. The workers have continually complained over the last two years about the safety conditions that exist in that area. They have complained to the provincial government and they have received no redress. Because this falls under the jurisdiction of the federal government they should have the right to ask the minister at least to intervene on their behalf in matters which are not covered by the provincial government but the responsibility for which may have been assumed by the provincial government. We believe that conditions, and particularly the safety factors, should be higher under the federal government than under the provincial government which has accepted the jurisdiction over the particular industry. When the federal government safety factors are higher, then they should apply, and I suggest this would be the case in the uranium mines of Blind River.

You have made two speeches this afternoon, sir, and I think you can wait until I am finished. Notwithstanding statements made by members of the government on many occasions, to say nothing of solemn promises made in the course of the election of last year, the unemployment situation is still grave enough to cause anxiety in many places, and anything that anyone can say to the contrary does not alter the fact that the situation is serious. I realize that the Minister of Labour has the matter of unemployment very much in mind and that he has tried to relieve it with the winter work program in co-operation with the municipalities and the provinces.
In the city of Fort William there are now approximately 100 persons working under the scheme but this is only a drop in the bucket in the face of some 2,760 still seeking employment at the present moment. Had it not been for the active co-operation which
Supply-Labour
the citizens of the community of Fort William have given to the winter do-it-now campaign, which is separate from the winter work program of the government, several hundred more would have been out of work all winter. Individual citizens, industry, business and labour are to be congratulated for their united support in assisting the effort put forth by the lakehead employment advisory committee. The members of this committee worked like beavers to create work.
I must also pay a compliment to the manager and staff of the national unemployment insurance office at Fort William for their untiring efforts in publicizing the need for co-operation. It is my belief that these campaigns fulfil a vital role during the winter months in assisting to create and spread employment to those who are unfortunately without the means of livelihood through no fault of their own. The success of these campaigns leaves no doubt that they are a part of our responsibility and a challenge that our economy must face and effectively solve. The suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition that a federal-provincial-municipal conference be held as soon as possible for the purpose of planning a winter work program for the next winter season is one that should be carried into effect without delay.
It is rather regrettable, and I am sure no one regrets it more than my good friend the Minister of Labour, who I must confess is sincere and hard working, but I must say that the government has not given evidence to date that it has an effective plan to deal with unemployment. I have no doubt that the government receives advice from many quarters because, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Welland this afternoon, advice is one of those commodities that are offered free of charge to anyone who wishes to listen. Nonetheless, sometimes there are some suggestions made which bear consideration. One of these appeared in the issue of the Globe and Mail of January 22, 1959 and I wish to read part of it for the record:
If one is to judge by recent discussions of economic problems, the nation has to take a choice between unemployment or inflation. Since inflation inevitably leads in the end to massive unemployment, it may seem there is no choice at all.
Fortunately, defeatism is not a Canadian characteristic and some of our better minds are not prepared to admit the impossibility of providing work for those who want to work constructively, and yet increasing real prosperity.
As something to think about, a proposal has been put forward by Eugen Berkovits, an international businessman and economist whose name has appeared in this column before. In his opinion, unemployment as a recurrent and urgent problem might be overcome by establishment of new manufacturing plants in this country on a large scale.

Evidence in support of his idea can be found in the way secondary industry has grown as a large employer here in recent years, far outstripping primary industry. If we would speed up that growth, says Mr. Berkovits, government might consider offering incentives and inducements, instead of having to make work itself and also make handouts to people who sooner would earn.
To this end, Mr. Berkovits suggests government should grant assistance to those who would establish new plants in Canada, in the way assistance is provided for housing, using the industrial development bank as the agency.
So the industrial development bank would be authorized to issue insurance policies in respect of industrial development loans granted by approved financial institutions, up to an aggregate of perhaps $1 billion. Industrial development bank would have the right of approval and each loan would be no greater than 80 per cent of the outlay necessary to get such new plants going. Repayment would be spread over 30 years, with a fee of possibly two per cent of the loan to cover the cost of insurance. Behind the industrial development bank would be the government-if required.
Mr. Berkovits does not believe government would get "caught" by such a guarantee system. New enterprises, as is well known, have a multiplying influence on production and between thus creating additional activity adding to the nation's wealth, the investment would start bringing back to gov-erment substantial taxes, so that the whole outlay might be balanced by income within four or five years. In contrast, housing loans, which also help employment, are not constant and expanding inducers of revenue.
While there might be a need for government to put up some money, as it has done for housing, Mr. Berkovits sees most of the capital under his plan coming from regular sources of funds, in greater volume when insurance reduces the risk.
This suggestion merits the consideration of the government and should be explored in every way. Our economic recovery depends to a very large degree on employment of human resources. The dangerous curves on the road to recovery are unemployment and inflation and these are the twins of misery which we must cope with, and so long as they are present so long will distress and unhappiness prevail.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, February 5, consideration of the motion of
