subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING STATUS OF NATURALIZED CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that when this bill was introduced on February 5, my friend the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge) late in the day moved an amendment which I want very warmly to support, namely that the bill should not be read a second time but that the subject matter thereof should be referred to the standing committee on external affairs. That motion was made after a previous motion that the bill should be referred to a special committee to be set up was found by the chair to be out of order. Of the standing committees, the external affairs committee therefore seemed the most closely related-although I admit it is not too closely related-to the subject matter of the bill. However, as we all know, it is a highly competent committee; and I am perfectly sure that if the subject matter of the bill were referred to it, the experience and the quality of the members on that committee would make them eminently well qualified to deal with the subject matter of this bill.
In introducing this bill originally I attempted to be as non-controversial as it is in my nature to be. It is not for me, of course, to be the judge of how well I succeeded. I found that some of the hon. gentlemen opposite were perhaps a little bit more controversial than I was or at least so it seemed to me. But I do not seek to say anything whatever about any of the personal references that were made to me or any of the objections that were taken to my administration of the department when I was the minister or to any of the other things of perhaps a not entirely complimentary nature that were said in that debate.
As I said at the outset, Mr. Speaker, it was my hope-and it is still my hope-that this matter could be considered and decided in a completely non-partisan manner in the best interests of all the people of Canada, for what we are talking about here is something that I trust all members in the House of Commons, to whatever party they may happen to belong, value equally. I refer to our common citizenship which I think binds all of us together more than anything divides us in this House of Commons, or at least that is my hope. I must say that I hope the hon. gentleman who is a learned member of his profession will not think it presumptuous of me, a student in the same profession, to say so but I thought the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk) was rather devastating in his legal criticisms of the bill.

In defence of the bill itself, I may say that it was drafted rather hastily in the house at the last session and was not revised. It was based upon an assertion that was made at that time by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough) to the effect that the particular matter to which it had reference was the only disability still existing in the act; that is to say, the only disability under which naturalized citizens suffered and natural born citizens did not. I thought that the hon. member for Marquette completely demonstrated that that foundation was wrong. The moment I heard him cite the section of the act that he cited, I realized that this bill was imperfect and that it would not be a proper bill to pass in the form in which it was introduced.
Of course, as hon. members will recall, I said at the outset that I was not in the least wedded to the terms of the bill, that I felt the purpose of the bill was clearly stated, that the principle of the bill was clear and that there would be no difficulty in revising the terms of the bill itself in a committee in order to fit the essential purpose that was in mind. However, in all the circumstances, I think it would be better to have the subject matter of the bill go to a committee where a new bill could be drafted based upon the principle of this bill.
I also thought that the hon. member for Marquette-I keep wanting to say "Portage" for some reason or other but I know it is "Marquette"-was quite right in thinking that the disability in section 18 should also be removed from the act. I think so too.
I want to go back to the real purpose of this bill. I want to say again-and try again to say this in a way that will not be controversial-that I do not think there was really any injustice in the old act as it was before it was amended at the last session of parliament. But there was a psychological situation that had developed. It seemed to me that on balance, the correcting of that psychological situation was more important than were the advantages of the old act. I think one can make a strong argument for the retention of section 18 in the citizenship act. But if you retain it or if you retain any other disability or any other difference between the legal status of a naturalized citizen and a natural born citizen, our citizenship is open to the charge that we have two kinds of citizens. In other words, it seemed to me that you must either do the whole job or there was really not much point in tampering with the act at all.
I come to the other argument of the hon. member for Marquette which I must say did not impress me nearly as much. I refer
66968-9-222
Canadian Citizenship Act to the argument that these persons who were still excepted by the one section of the act which I was seeking to have amended do not deserve to carry the honourable name of "Canadian" and, of course, I quite agree. I quite agree that if, in fact, they are the kind of people it would be charged that they were, that is quite true. But I am afraid there are many other citizens who do not deserve to carry the honourable name of "Canadian". You either have discrimination or you do not have discrimination. You cannot have almost no discrimination and have equality. That is one of those mathematical propositions on which I am sure the hon. member and I would not disagree. It therefore seems to me that either one has to do what hon. gentlemen opposite or some of their leaders before the election in 1957 said they would do, or not do it. If you do not do it, we would probably be just as well off-in fact, I am not sure that we would not have been better off with the old act-and I am going to explain briefly why.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. MacLean), who also made, I thought, a very interesting, illuminating, thoughtful and scholarly contribution to the debate, on which I would like, if he will not take offence, to congratulate him, pointed out something which had never occurred to me when I was minister as being a discrimination, but obviously is once it is pointed out. That is that there were certain kinds of so-called natural born citizens, although they were not born in this country, who did not have an equality with the natural born citizens who were born in this country. It is quite clear that if this task of establishing a status of complete legal equality is going to be performed, it does require a careful examination of the whole act. It seems to me that that would be very well worth doing and there would be no harm in going ahead with it in anticipation of the wider study of the act which we hope there will be at the next session of parliament.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, however, did make another argument which did not impress me nearly as much as the legal argument he made, and that was his argument about the desirability of retaining the disability which is now in the act to which the bill has reference. The hon. gentleman was arguing that it was very important to be able to strip of their citizenship those Canadians who, on being accused of treason, left the country or were not in the country and would not come back to stand trial. I think a lot can be said in favour of that, but surely there is just as much to be said in favour of stripping of their citizenship those people who have been convicted

Canadian Citizenship Act of treason or of disloyalty to the country and who, after serving their sentence, leave the country and sever their connection with it for a considerable period of time. As hon. members know, that was the law up till it was changed by the present government a year ago.
At the time I was minister a very celebrated case arose. It was the case of a man who had been a member of this house at one time and who had subsequently been convicted in the courts, who after serving his sentence, had left the country and gone to live in the country where he was born, who had lived there for the statutory period and on whom I caused to be served the necessary legal instrument, who appealed against my announced intention of recommending that his citizenship be stripped from him, and whose appeal was listened to and dismissed. I am not using these terms in a legal sense, of course, but rather in an administrative sense. I then recommended that his citizenship be taken from him, and the governor in council saw fit to accept that recommendation and that person lost his citizenship. That is not possible any longer. Since the law was amended by the present government, that person would retain his citizenship although he had been convicted, had served a sentence, and then had gone out of the country with the apparent intention of severing his connection with it. In that case we could not now take his citizenship away from him.
It seems to me that since the present government saw fit to remove from the act the possibility of taking citizenship away from a person of that sort, it is very illogical indeed to retain in the act this other disability of removing citizenship from a person who has never been convicted of anything, against whom a charge has been laid but who does not see fit to come back and have the charge heard. It might be conceivable, in spite of the very best efforts which might be made to find him and acquaint him with the charge, that he might not be aware of the charge or the circumstances. I must say that it does seem a little odd that it should be argued by hon. gentlemen, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre seemed to argue-and when I asked him a question he told me I was trying to wriggle out of it, but it struck me that the wriggling was all being done not by me but by the hon. gentleman-in view of the fact that later this session hon. members will presumably be supporting a bill of rights which we are told in the speech from the throne is to be introduced by the leader of the government, that it would be wise to maintain disabilities against a person who has never been tried but remove disabilities

against someone who has been tried and convicted. It is rather an odd conception of equality of rights. I do think myself that there is a very strong argument for taking citizenship away from people like that. There is also a strong argument for equality. It is an argument that induced me to introduce this bill, and notwithstanding the strong arguments on the other side, left in my mind a balance in favour of making all Canadians legally equal. I must say I am unrepentant in the views that that is what we should do.
The hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl), with approval from some other hon. members, did suggest that there was another way of doing it, and that was to impose disabilities upon natural born citizens and to strip them of their citizenship in certain circumstances.
I do not think that we would ever get this parliament to do that, and I do not think we would ever get parliament to do it for this reason. When we strip those people of their citizenship we would be making stateless persons out of them deliberately. In the case of some naturalized persons, what we are doing is simply restoring to them the citizenship which they had before, though in some cases we are not. Again I think that is another important consideration. The idea of making outlaws of individuals is to my mind very reprehensible and completely out of accord with the notions of jurisprudence which exist today in most of the civilized countries of the free world. It seems to me that this is another very strong argument for our bringing the law completely up to date in this regard. I must say that in all the circumstances I do feel that by one means or another we should try very hard in this parliament to reach agreement in regard to equality of citizenship.
Another point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was this. I do not want to take up a lot of time in reading over the previous debate, although if the hon. gentleman thinks I misrepresent anything he said, I would be only too glad to be corrected at once because, as I say, I am seeking to be completely fair and uncontroversial. The hon. member raised the question of fraud. It seems to me that a person who gets a citizenship certificate by fraud has not in fact become a citizen. I think we should deal with such cases judicially. The determination of the facts as to whether he got his certificate by fraud would be a matter, I think, not for any government but for the courts. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre seemed to think that that would make the law more rigid than if some administrative discretion were allowed. I think this is a judicial matter.
No minister should have it in his power to decide whether someone else is guilty of fraud. That is what we have law courts for,

and if that is going to be done at all I am sure that is the way it should be done. Of course, it may be that the language of the drafting was not all it should be, but I think the hon. gentleman would find that using the word "court" meant whatever was the court of competent jurisdiction with whatever rights of appeal there would be. I would think that there should be all the rights of appeal that there would be in many other similar kinds of cases. I can see that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was, I think, properly concerned about one problem, because there is a problem here. It is conceivable that someone might 20 years ago have obtained a certificate of citizenship or, as it used to be called 20 years ago, naturalization, not having complied with the law. That person, during all this long period would have been regarded as a Canadian citizen, and it would seem to me-and I thank the hon. gentleman for putting this idea in my head-that we would not want to frame the law in such a way that notwithstanding the fact that that man never really became a citizen he would have to start all over again and be landed as an immigrant, if that was necessary, and have to wait for another five years before he could become a citizen.
I do think the hon. member has found another gap which ought to be filled. It is a gap which, I imagine, exists as much in the existing law as in the one suggested. Some provision should be made in cases where either there was good faith in the beginning or good conduct in the country since that time-some process by which citizenship could be conferred with a very slight delay indeed.
Perhaps the court could be given the power to make that kind of favourable decision on application immediately after an adverse decision had been reached in the other case if it seemed desirable.
It seems to me those were the only points of substance which were raised. I looked over the debate the other day when I thought this matter was coming up but it did not come up because of our higher interest in divorce which I am sure is a matter of great interest in some parts of this country at the present time. I am not going to detain the house any longer but I am going to appeal to hon. members to bring this matter to a vote, because all it will do is to send this subject matter to a committee where we can perhaps have a preliminary canter over the subject. In view of the complexities which have been revealed during the debate I do not think we would probably reach a decision this session, but I think it might be 66968-9-222J

He has not satisfied my mind as to the need for this amendment, or the reasons why it is being introduced by him at this time after his term of office as minister of citizenship and immigration. While he occupied that position I do not think there were any major amendments made to the Canadian Citizenship Act, and I am sure that citizenship in those years was as important to Canadians as it is today.
I have been connected with the newly formed citizenship council in the province of Manitoba, and the discussions that they are having and the problems that they are encountering in getting their organization on its feet and in trying to promote better citizenship in this country. They certainly are not having any problems with people outside of Canada who have been charged with treason. This is a very small and insignificant matter when you consider the whole matter of citizenship in its entirety. There is no discrimination in Canada between natural born Canadians and naturalized Canadians. If there is any discrimination in our act at all it does not affect citizens who are in Canada; it affects Canadian citizens who are outside of Canada. In my estimation, that is a more important point. When we consider that a great many countries of this world allow dual citizenship-by that I mean citizens of those countries can come to Canada and obtain their Canadian citizenship and still retain citizenship in the country from which they came-this puts us into a difficult position, or it could put us into a difficult position in certain circumstances and in certain instances. For example, a person who has such dual citizenship could come to Canada and commit an offence which would prompt our law officials to lay a charge of treason, and then leave the country and refuse to return to stand trial. In such a situation we would have a citizen who could go all over his native land or into countries which are ideologically opposed to us and brag about being a Canadian citizen. I for one do not like to think of that happening. I do not know whether it would ever happen but I suggest that just because the incidence of occurrence may be very small that is no argument for removing something from the statute books.
[Mr. MacLean (Winnipeg North Centre) .1
I think we should have certain protections on our statute books to provide a deterrent or a punishment for situations that could arise in the future which might be embarrassing to us as far as our neighbours in the world community are concerned. I might even go so far as to agree with the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) when he says that a natural-born Canadian citizen should also lose his citizenship under the same circumstances. I would be inclined to agree with him except for the fact that we should be creating a person with a stateless category. That is something that is repugnant to our way of thinking and it is something that I would certainly have to do a lot more thinking about before I would permit myself to advocate it.
In this country we have a certain amount of pro-communism and a great deal of anticommunism. I think the anti-communist element is more pronounced in those communities which are made up of new Canadians or naturalized Canadians. I do not hesitate to say that if any naturalized Canadian found himself within the confines of the section of the Canadian Citizenship Act that we are discussing today his fellow naturalized Canadians would not have too much sympathy for him; for these people have seen what happens in countries where persons sell their souls and their morals to a political philosophy that in effect means slavery and means imprisonment and lack of freedom. They have seen this happen first-hand. One of the main reasons why many of them came to this country was to get away from places where that could happen. I would think that possibly, instead of worrying ourselves today with how we are going to treat people who are charged with treason we should be worrying ourselves as to how we are going to, or whether or not it would be a good idea to get rid of certain people in our society who are trouble-makers and who are openly opposed to the democratic system as we know it.
I am not by any means advocating expulsion because one holds a communistic belief or a socialistic belief, but I would think we would be much better off discussing that point, or discussing how we can help new Canadians rather than discussing how or whether we should deal with people charged with treason in the manner in which this act stipulates.

Mr. Speaker, it is a known fact that one-third of Canada's population is either naturalized or descended from naturalized Canadians. These people came from all parts of the world and they have helped to pioneer and develop this land. They have contributed to every part of the economy of the country. Men and women who change their minds about Canada, men and women who get sour on Canada, men and women who have come into this country with bad intentions, these are the only ones likely to run afoul of cancellation clauses.

subtopic: CABINET COMMITTEE AUTHORIZATIONS
CABINET COMMITTEE AUTHORIZATIONS
speechtext:
1.	Are orders in council in effect at the present time authorizing cabinet committees, ad hoc cabinet committees, committees of council, and interdepartmental committees?
2.	If so, what are the numbers and dates and contents of the particular orders in council?
3.	Who are the members of these committees?
Answer by: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker
(Prime Minister):
1.	Cabinet committees have no legal powers and are set up from time to time by the cabinet without any orders in council.
There are two committees of the privy council, both authorized and given certain powers by statute. These are the treasury board, established by the Financial Administration Act, and the committee of the privy council on scientific and industrial research, established by the Research Council Act. In addition, there is a statutory committee of which certain ministers of the crown are members, together with the Speaker of the House of Commons. This is the committee of internal economy, provided for in the House of Commons Act.
In the past, interdepartmental committees were set up from time to time by order in council but the present practice is for them to be established by the cabinet, by the treasury board or by the minister or ministers most directly concerned. There is still one active interdepartmental committee, the establishment and terms of reference of which were authorized by order in council. This is the standing committee on public records, of which a minister is chairman.
2.	Present members and alternates of the treasury board were appointed by orders in council P.C. 1957-889, of June 21, P.C. 19571188 of August 29, and P.C. 1958-1326 of September 22. Present members of the scientific and industrial research committee were appointed by order in council P.C. 1958-1482 of October 23. Present members of the internal economy committee were appointed by order in council P.C. 1958-1715 of December 17. The committee on public records was set up by order in council P.C. 6175 of September 20, 1945, and its composition is set out therein, subject to the changes that have taken place in ministerial responsibility. Copies of the above orders are attached.
3.	Answered by (2) above.

THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL:
WHEREAS the secretary of state reports that, at the request of the Prime Minister he has convened an informal advisory committee on public records to give consideration to methods for providing adequate conservation of the public records, with particular

reference to those records relating to the wartime activities of the government; and
That, following investigation of the state of the public records, a report has been prepared and considered by the committee and certain recommendations resulting therefrom approved;
Now, therefore, his excellency the governor general in council, on the recommendation of the Secretary of State, is pleased to order and doth hereby order as follows:-
1.	There shall be a committee on public records under the chairmanship of the Secretary of State and consisting of the following officials:-
A representative to be named by the Secretary of State (public archives).
Two representatives to be named by the Minister of National Defence (army and naval services).
A representative to be named by the Minister of National Defence-Air.
A representative to be named by the Minister of Public Works.
A representative to be named by the Minister of Finance.
A representative to be named by the minister of munitions and supply and the minister of reconstruction.
A representative to be named by the Minister of Labour.
A representative to be named by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
A secretary shall be provided from the privy council office.
2.	The Canadian Historical Association shall be asked to recommend two professional historians to act in an advisory capacity to the committee to serve at no salary but with expenses to be provided by the government.
3.	The duties of the committee shall be to keep under constant review the state of the public records and to consider, advise and concert with departments and agencies of government on the organization, care, housing, and destruction of public records.
4.	The committee shall, as part of their duties, examine and report on the following:
(a)	The preparation by departments and agencies of government of suitable accounts of their wartime activities and,
(b)	The implementing of the approved recommendations of the royal commission on public records of 1914 regarding establishment of a public records office, with particular reference to the integration of the
Questions
public archives therein, and the type of organization which would facilitate the best use of the public records.
5.	When questions specifically affecting the records of a department are being dealt with, a representative from that department shall be present at the meeting.
6.	The primary responsibility for the care and maintenance of records and for seeing that the policies of government in respect to disposition of public records be carried out so as to ensure that material of permanent value be not unwittingly destroyed will rest with departments and agencies of government concerned.
7.	Each department shall assign responsibility for superintendence of its records to one or more senior officers, preferably the departmental secretary if such a position exists, or an official of similar rank. The duties of these officers will be to review periodically the state of the departmental records and to reclassify them with a view to disposal or transfer of those of permanent value but not currently required to the public archives (or public records office, if established) or to other dominion or provincial departments, or by some form of destruction under existing regulations. These officers will also maintain liaison with agencies responsible to the minister. Recommendations respecting contemplated disposal along the above lines shall be submitted, in all cases, for formal approval of the committee on public records.

subtopic: STRONTIUM 90    TABLING OF REPORT ON EFFECTS OF RADIOACTIVE FALL-OUT

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monteith (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: STRONTIUM 90    TABLING OF REPORT ON EFFECTS OF RADIOACTIVE FALL-OUT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some weeks ago I intimated to the house that my department's next regular report on strontium 90 levels in milk powder samples was expected shortly. This has now been completed, and is being distributed through the usual channels. In view of the widespread interest in the subject I should also like to table it for the information of hon. members. The report contains new data on milk covering the period April to December, 1958. It is the second in a series of reports which will deal with the
measurements of radioactive fall-out in air, rainfall, soil, various foods and in human beings.
While the report speaks for itself, I think certain points warrant special mention. Of first importance is the fact that our findings indicate no basis for alarm about this matter. Although it is evident that the strontium 90 levels have continued to increase, it is made clear that they are well below the stringent standards suggested by international authorities.
I am also aware that there continues to be concern about the stress given to milk in this regard, and I would emphasize again that milk was chosen for sampling because of its convenience and because it is an important item in our daily diet. In addition, dairy products provide most of our food calcium, the absorption of which by the body is closely associated with the absorption of strontium 90. At the present time our findings, taken together with other available information on the biological effects of radiation, provide no basis for curtailment of the use of dairy products.
At this point I would remind the house that radioactive fall-out constitutes only one of several sources of radiation exposure for Canadians. Other man-made radiation sources have been in use for at least half a century and, moreover, the human race has always been exposed to radiation from natural sources. Estimates have been made of the relative contributions to the average radiation exposure from each of these sources, and it is apparent that radioactive fall-out contributes only a small part of the total.
In order to evaluate more completely the over-all situation we plan to expand our radiation protection activities in several ways. Currently we are extending our fall-out sampling program to include analyses of air, rainfall and soil. We are also engaged in a study of the genetically significant dose resulting from the medical use of X-rays. At a later stage we propose to investigate the variations in natural radiation levels. The results of these studies, as they become available, will be the basis of further reports.

subtopic: STRONTIUM 90    TABLING OF REPORT ON EFFECTS OF RADIOACTIVE FALL-OUT
speechtext:
This is a matter which is, of course, of the greatest importance. The minister has said in effect that the strontium level does not appreciably increase any danger to human health. How-

Inquiries of the Ministry ever, he has pointed out that strontium levels themselves continue to increase. That is a matter, of course, of great concern to the minister and I am sure to his officials, as it is to scientists generally. The house and the country would expect the government and the minister to give this matter their closest attention.
The minister has mentioned that there has been an expansion in the radioactive detection facilities and activities of his department. I presume that includes the purchase of new equipment, reference to which was made by Dr. Watkinson about two months ago. Perhaps the minister might supplement his statement by advising whether or not the facilities of the government have been reinforced by the employment of at least one additional geneticist.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON U.S. ASSISTANCE RESPECTING NUCLEAR-POWERED VESSELS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON U.S. ASSISTANCE RESPECTING NUCLEAR-POWERED VESSELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Leader of the Opposition asked me the following question:
There appears in today's press the news of an agreement between the United States and the United Kingdom under which, according to the report, the United States has agreed to furnish information to the United Kingdom regarding the design and construction of a nuclear-powered submarine. The United States has already agreed to provide a reactor for a British nuclear-powered submarine. I should like to ask the Prime Minister if there is any arrangement for that kind of co-operation and assistance if required between the United States and Canada in connection with not only a nuclear-powered submarine but a nuclear-powered icebreaker if one were required?
As I stated on April 21, negotiations have been proceeding with the government of the United States with a view to modification of the 1955 agreement on the exchange of atomic information for mutual defence purposes, to take account of the amendments to the relevant United States legislation which was passed in July of 1958.
I am very glad to say that the government is confident that as a consequence of the bilateral agreement which is now being negotiated, the way would be open to make arrangements for the kind of co-operation and assistance which would be required if the government of Canada were to decide to build a nuclear-powered submarine. However, the cost would have to be taken into consideration. I understand the cost runs to something like $60 million.
So far as a nuclear-powered icebreaker is concerned, information regarding a project for the non-military use of a reactor such as, for instance, to supply power for such a vessel could be exchanged by mutual agreement between Canada and the United States within the scope of the agreement on co-operation in the civil uses of atomic energy.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister if he is in a position to advise the house as to what attitude the government has taken with regard to the reported request by India and Poland for a reconvening of the international supervisory committee on truce arrangements in Laos.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minisler):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF SUPERVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been differences of opinion over the possibility of attempting to reconvene the international commission for Laos which was adjourned sine die on July 19, 1958. Early this year a request for the reconvening of this commission came from the Poles, who urged resumption of the commission's activities in Laos on the ground that the commission should continue to carry out its supervisory functions there. North Viet Nam and communist China also requested a resumption of the Laos commission's activities. In December, 1958 north Viet Namese incursions into Laotian territory occurred. The Indian government, following upon this frontier dispute, urged a meeting of the Laos commission to deal with this specific problem.
Hon. members may also have seen press reports to the effect that the Soviet embassy in London handed a note to the foreign office on April 29 requesting the return of the international commission to Laos. The Canadian government received a similar request

from the Soviet ambassador on April 28. It will be recalled that the United Kingdom and Soviet foreign ministers are the joint co-chairmen of the Geneva conference, and in that capacity act as a channel of communication with the international commissions in Indochina.
During the negotiations leading up to the adjournment sine die of the Laos commission in July, 1958 the Canadian position was that with the achievement of the political settlement in Laos and the integration of the dissident Pathet Lao into the national community, the commission had completed its supervisory task and should be dissolved. Because the Indian representatives did not accept that view, Canada agreed to the compromise formula of an adjournment sine die against the opposition of the Poles. However, the Canadian commissioner was instructed to make it quite clear, at the final meeting of the commission, that Canada could not agree to any further commission action which would infringe upon Laotian sovereignty.
I understand that the government of Laos is opposed to the reconvening of the commission. The Polish request, in the view of the Canadian government, did not bring forward adequate reasons for reconvening the commission, and since it called for a reconstitution of the commission secretariat in Vientiane, it would have been an obvious infringement on Laotian sovereignty.
I think that in general represents the situation at this time.

speechtext:
I wish to make a few remarks on this item-and I shall try to be brief-with respect to the problem of unemployment which exists at the present time and may be worse next winter. We in this group consider that unemployment in a country like Canada is a serious injustice to those who suffer by it. In the second place, it is an unnecessary waste of human resources. In the third place, it is a challenge to governments in general at all levels, to industry, to labour and to the people as a whole.
66968-9-220
Supply-Labour
Personally I believe it is unthinkable to accept the dictum that we must accept a hard core of unemployment in Canada throughout the year, and that that core should be larger during the winter because of seasonal unemployment.
During the last session of the British Columbia legislature the labour committee gave considerable consideration to this problem as it affects British Columbia. That committee was composed of representatives from all parties, and I am informed that it made a unanimous report to the legislature. I want to bring to the attention of the committee at this time a portion of that report with respect to its recommendations concerning the national government.
The committee invited representations from labour, industry and other sections of the community. It received briefs and representations from the British Columbia federation of labour; the mine, mill and smelter workers representing the miners of British Columbia, and other unions. It heard from various sections of industry through employers' representatives. It heard from the alma mater society of the University of British Columbia, which organization in my opinion made a thoughtful presentation. It heard from the research council of British Columbia, and finally it heard from some of the minister's officials in the regional offices at the coast.
In dealing with this question, Mr. Chairman, the committee considered all aspects of the problem-and I thought they did so in a constructive way-and dealt with the extent of unemployment in British Columbia from January, 1957 to January, 1959. They then sought to find the major causes of unemployment in British Columbia during 1958, and then made certain proposals as to the responsibility of the national government, the provincial government, the local governments, the trade union movement and industry.
I want just to place on record the recommendations of the committee with respect to responsibilities, from the committee's point of view, of the national government to meet this situation. In the report of the committee on labour of the legislative assembly of British Columbia, dated March 18, 1959 this is what I read with respect to the responsibilities of the national government. The committee had this to recommend:
I.	The national government
By virtue of its control over the collections and disbursements of unemployment insurance funds, as well as constitutionally within the framework of the British North America Act as accepted by the national government when taking over certain taxation privileges from provincial administration, the primary responsibility for employment in

Supply-Labour
Canada rests with the national government. With that authority lies the power to sustain a climate conducive to industrial expansion and the creation of new industries with a consequent high level of employment of the working force. Specifically, your committee considers that the national government of Canada should:-
1.	Materially assist in a large-scale works program at appropriate times of the year on such projects as:
(a)	Forest access, transprovincial, and interprovincial roads:
(b)	Park and campsite improvement;
(c)	Diking and drainage projects;
(d)	Stream clearance projects and the creation of artificial spawning areas;
(In this latter connection it is contended that, since the improvement of fishways on the Fraser river eight years ago at a cost of $2 million, the salmon yield has increased by $127 million at cannery prices, and it is therefore evident that such projects would in time be self-liquidating because of the tremendous dollar market value increase in a comparatively short period of time.)
(e)	Fraser river flood control consistent with a policy of fish conservation.
Then No. 2; the committee recommends that the federal government:
2.	Institute an enlarged program of apprenticeship and trades training during adverse seasons of employment by extending the scope of the unemployment insurance commission.
Mr. Chairman, I have had a good number of representations along those lines which I intend to deal with when we are discussing the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. It goes on:
3.	Adopt a carefully screened immigration policy on the basis of the stated needs of industry and agriculture thus ensuring the planned assimilation of immigrants into the national working force.
4.	Encourage and promote the construction of coastal shipping and national defence requirements in Canada.
5.	Foster the expansion of a research program designed to encourage the use of coal and coal by-products in our industrial economy.
No doubt that recommendation, Mr. Chairman, springs from the fact that the coal industry in British Columbia, particularly in the Fernie area, is suffering a decline at this time.
6.	Initiate the formation of a joint federal-provincial trade investigation team to the republic of China for the purpose of inquiring into trade possibilities with that country.
I would like to bring to the minister's attention that this recommendation was made both by industry and labour, because the working people of British Columbia as well as the industrial interests realize the great possibility of expansion of our markets for primary products if we can obtain greater trade in that direction.
7.	To provide the ways and means to extend low cost credit in order to:-
(a) Promote and expand economic development and stimulate revenue, income, or self-liquidating projects or works by the province and its municipalities; and to
[Mr. Herridge.)
(b) Assist and encourage the establishment and growth of local industries.
Then, Mr. Chairman, the last recommendation is:
8.	Give leadership and co-operation in the calling of a federal-provincial conference to seek a Canada-wide solution to the unemployment problem, requesting representation from all levels of government.
Now, Mr. Chairman, while I heartily support the proposal of the committee for a federal-provincial conference including all levels of government, I think for such a conference to be effective in providing a clear picture of the situation, and at the same time adequately representing the view of the Canadian people generally, that conference should also include representatives from labour, from industry, and from agriculture across this country.
When I say representation, I mean decentralized representation. I am a great believer, Mr. Chairman, that in the development of our domestic society we should decentralize authority and administration. I would like to see all sections of labour have the opportunity to be represented at such a conference. For instance, I think all sections of labour from the Atlantic to the Pacific, such as the forestry industry, the mining industry, the steel industry and the oil industry, should be represented. Then you would have a conference where the government would get the rank and file point of view in dealing with these day to day and very important problems.
The same thing, I think, Mr. Chairman, applies to industry. It is not sufficient just to call in the Canadian Manufacturers Association and have two or three big shots express their views. We have a diversified industrial structure in Canada, and I would like to see at such a conference representatives of various sections of industry, including the small industries, from every province in Canada, and in that way you would get all the information these people would be able to give.
Then with regard to farming, I would like to see a diversified representation in the same way, so that the grain farmers, the general farmers, the dairy farmers, the fruit farmers and the poultry farmers would be all represented at such a conference on a diversified basis, instead of having two or three people speaking for the whole industry. That would give the conference and the government a clear picture not only on a national or a provincial basis but also on a local basis.
Before taking my seat, Mr. Chairman, I would like to bring another matter to the minister's attention. I see he is busy chatting at the present time but I hope he will read my remarks later on. I am not blaming him

entirely for this, because I think the blame can rest in other quarters too. But I would like to bring to his attention the success which has been achieved in this direction in the little country of Norway. I have recently been reading some books about the Norwegian government, for which I have a great respect. I have a great respect for all Norwegians. They are a simple and resourceful people who have had to meet some great problems both in peace and in war, and they have met them successfully, and I think countries of our size can learn from such lesser countries, countries with more experience and possibly more maturity when it comes to handling the organizations which represent the various groups of society.
I have been very interested to note how they have formed just such an advisory council representing industry, labour and agriculture in order to deal with the problems of inflation, monetary fiscal policy, unemployment, industry and economy generally. Their conferences have been called somewhat on the basis I have suggested this morning, so they get the local rank and file touch in meeting these problems.
I think that is a principle which can be explored to advantage in Canada. In this way not only does the government get the opinion of various sections of labour, industry and agriculture, but the persons who have the opportunity to represent these people also learn the problems of government and the difficulties which have to be faced. Out of this blending of ideas, this association of different interests, which has such a constructive approach to the problems facing us at this time can be evolved, as was done in Norway, a program which will receive the support of all classes of the people. I do urge the minister to give consideration to a conference of that type.
In addition I think other advantages flow from that type of conference. All programs have to be financed, and when it comes to bond issues for capital investment in self-liquidating projects, I think flowing from such a conference would come an understanding of the problems which face the government and a greater understanding of the program the government may desire to carry out. But it is desirable to have this local interest.
For instance, if I may refer to a local industry in my own district, say the government intended to do certain things with respect to access roads or provincial roads as the result of a program designed to meet the challenge of unemployment. In that case, if you floated a bond issue I think even in the smallest communities of Canada there would be people who would, under those 66968-9-220J
Supply-Labour
circumstances, willingly purchase government bonds to assist in such a program because of their greater knowledge of the circumstances and the need, and also because of their interest which would spring from local participation in the development of that program. I think it would be most beneficial in designing a program to get an understanding of it, and from that I think would flow quite an interest in assisting to provide some of the funds which are necessary to give effect to such a program. Many more people would then feel that they were a part of this program and that they should accept some personal responsibility by making what financial contribution they could toward any bond issues which were offered to meet any of the challenges of national development at this time.
That is all I have to say at this time, and I put the suggestion forward as a constructive approach toward meeting the problem of unemployment as it faces us today.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF SUPERVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Like other members of this committee I am very much concerned about those Canadians who are unemployed. I am afraid we refer to them some times rather blandly as mere statistics, forgetting that they are human beings with human problems and human needs. I think the time for taking practical steps in an effort to alleviate their position is overdue. It is not my intention to give a lecture on economics or to talk about the situation in a general sense. I wish, rather, to put forward a specific proposal.
I am becoming more and more distressed about the situation of the unemployed. When I go home at week ends I talk to many people, some are young, some middle aged, some of them older, some of them skilled, some of them without any skill or training at all. Each has a common problem. Each is unemployed. Many of these people have mortgage payments which are overdue. Many of them have doctor bills and other bills to meet. Many have family responsibilities and must keep a roof over the heads of their children. Almost every week end I talk to some person who has just lost, or is just about to lose, his home because of inability to meet the financial obligations connected with it.
Chronic unemployment makes cynics, petty crooks and communists out of decent people, and in a rich, young and dynamic economy such as we have in Canada it should be a fundamental right of any able bodied man to be able to work at a wage which will keep body and soul together and provide not only for himself but for his family. Our task as elected representatives who come here to take cognizance of the needs of the people we

Supply-Labour
represent is to try to determine what solutions are best able to meet this grievous situation. Our task is to maintain employment and, through employment, the values of human dignity and decency.
The problem is very difficult to solve completely. As is well known, a significant proportion of our unemployment is seasonal. Many improvements have been made in this respect in the last few years. There have been great strides in technology, and dislocation due to seasonal unemployment is, I think, diminishing. Great strides will be made in the future, and we should press forward in research and study in an effort to find every means possible of mitigating still further the effects of seasonal unemployment.
I think, however, it would be too much to expect that we could ever completely overcome this problem which is indigenous to our climatic conditions. We experience, in addition, the type of unemployment which is called frictional, by which is meant people changing their jobs in the normal course of events. This is something we will always have with us, and something which need not cause us too much concern.
In our search for a solution to this whole problem we require the fullest possible information. The statistics available at present do not give us the whole story. I think we need more detailed information and a more careful study. In approaching this question seriously I feel that the first step required would be a national manpower survey. How extensive this survey ought to be should be left to the experts to determine, but the survey would have to accomplish certain things. It would have to give us a complete analysis of the unemployed labour force, it should determine into which age categories the unemployed workers fall, and give us a more complete breakdown of a variety of information including marital status, training, educational background, vocational training background and, perhaps, job history; sufficient information to enable us to tackle the problem in an all-out manner. It should not be difficult for the national employment service and the unemployment insurance commission to obtain all this information. It would, of course, be an additional job for them at a time when they are already overtaxed, but it is one which is within their capacity and one for which they have the machinery in being.
If such a survey were made, we should then know accurately how many of those people registered as seeking employment were actually unemployed. We should know whether they were plumbers, carpenters, nurses, stenographers, unskilled labourers.
We should know just what their background happened to be. We should know the extent of their educational background, whether they had completed grade school, high school, college; whether they had received apprenticeship training or vocational training; whether they had been self-taught, or whether they had received no training at all. I am sure it would be possible for the commission to obtain sufficient information along these lines to provide material for a very careful and detailed analysis.
At the same time it would be necessary to make a study of the extent and nature of job openings in this country. We should seek to determine what skills will be required not only at the present time but in the months and years which lie ahead. Employers can give a great deal of assistance in this respect. Most of them can forecast their requirements at least for a year or two ahead, and know the type of jobs they are likely to have available. Such information as this is, of course, essential. Whether or not it would be necessary to cover the entire working force in connection with this survey is something I am not prepared to say. That is a decision which can be taken by the people who make these matters their day to day business. The survey should be just as broad as is required to enable us to obtain all the information necessary to meet the situation fully and do the job properly.
The question may be asked, if this is a good suggestion why was it not done some years ago? I think if it were a good suggestion then, it is a good suggestion now. Moreover, the problem is of greater urgency today than it was previously, due to the increase in unemployment since the summer of 1957. Besides, this is a matter which is far too important for quibbling. Completion of such a study as I have suggested would provide facts and eliminate reliance on hearsay.
We are told, for instance, that a great number of those who are at present unemployed are of a mature age and that as a consequence they find a great deal of difficulty in obtaining employment. We are told day after day that people over 40 find difficulty in obtaining employment due to company pension plans. I have no doubt that this is true, but we should know specifically to what extent it is true. If necessary we should examine individual pension plans and find out which provisions make it difficult for employers to engage people over 40. It may be we shall need to do some rethinking and take the initiative in making changes in the pension plans which now exist.
I am sure, and I know the minister agrees with me, that it was not the intention of

either management or labour to set up these pension plans in such a way as to constitute a deterrent to the employment of mature and experienced workers and keep them from rejoining the labour force. This is something which might have been done inadvertently; it would not have been done deliberately. If this should be the case it is our responsibility to find out about it and take the initiative in changing whatever has to be changed.
Another common complaint we hear is that many of the people seeking employment are incompletely or inadequately trained. It is difficult to know to what extent this is true. One suspects from interviewing people that there is considerable validity to this statement. Our survey would show whether or not there is correlation between training and employment, and to what extent lack of training is responsible for unemployment.
Many people in the unemployed labour force went into the labour market in the early post-war years. This was a natural thing to do. Many went in without finishing their schooling. The attraction at the time was very great; high wages prevailed, and it was easy for almost anyone to get a job. This tended to seduce people from their academic or professional studies and persuaded them to enter the labour force perhaps earlier than they would have done in other times. These people now lack the training which they would have had in the ordinary course of events, and for them there is a special problem.
We hear from day to day that for the employment opportunities that do exist there are not skilled applicants. I have personal knowledge of some of these cases. I mentioned earlier this session a period last summer when there were not sufficient trained plasterers to meet the demand. Just two weeks ago in Toronto I was talking to a coat manufacturer who had openings for three machine operators. He was unable to hire adequately trained machine operators. I also know that in the construction industry there could be openings for highly skilled estimators, inspectors, material handlers, material expediters and for other classes of people if they had sufficient technological training to fill openings of this kind. There must be many other trades and vocations where there are employment opportunities if the people were available who had the training and skills required.
In the unemployed labour force at the present time there undoubtedly are a number of skilled workers whose skills may be in overabundant supply or for whose skills there may be continually contracting requirement. This is a situation that is likely to continue in
Supply

Labour
the wake of automation. Inevitably there will be change, and our responsibility is to face it and use it to our national advantage.
We should not attempt to impede the progress of automation, from which a great deal of dislocation can be expected and much adjustment will be necessary. Automation will be a great boon and a blessing if we are prepared to plan for it and use our displaced personnel to the best advantage of the total economy and channel their productivity and creative talents into new, productive enterprises and outlets. This is a program that will require some imagination. It is a problem that has not existed for very long and one to which we perhaps have not given sufficient attention. It will require imaginative and well-planned study. This is a problem which I know we can and will face and solve if we really set our minds to it.
Once the facts had been determined by our survey the next step would be to launch a massive rehabilitation program. It seems ironic that during wartime big men present big plans and achieve big success with almost universal public support, whereas in peacetime we seem reluctant to face big problems and procrastinate sometimes almost interminably in seeking solutions. If we could just maintain some of that sense of urgency which we feel during wartime we could achieve miracles.
This program of massive rehabilitation could be patterned on the experience gained by the Department of Veterans Affairs in the early post-war years. At that time, as you will recall, the government made it possible for veterans to undertake academic or vocational training at government expense. More than 60,000 veterans took some university training under that plan, and almost 100,000 were approved for vocational training. Many, of course, did not complete their studies, but there is no doubt but that they have been able to contribute much more to the growth and potential of the Canadian economy as a result of the opportunity made available to them.
The massive rehabilitation program would, in effect, be a massive program of adult education. It could be set up in various centres right across Canada from Newfoundland to British Columbia. The number of trades and subjects taught would, of course, be related both to the demand for these particular courses and to the result of the survey and future surveys held from time to time, indicating the extent to which any trade or skill would be required in the economy. Participants would be given complete freedom of choice in their selection,

Supply-Labour
but it would probably be advisable to provide counselling service. In addition, though I personally am somewhat leery of them, aptitude tests could be given if requested.
I do not know why persons drawing unemployment insurance and for whom there is no immediate prospect of job openings should not take advantage of the opportunity to increase their knowledge or improve their skills. I am confident that many would welcome the opportunity. In many cases, no doubt, it would be a first introduction to vocational or technical training; in other cases an extension or supplement to previous courses. For others it would be the commencement of acquiring a new skill as an alternative to one already possessed which is in oversupply. Such a plan, of course, would not necessarily be limited to those persons drawing unemployment insurance but should be available to those on municipal relief, etc.
It may be said that there is a constitutional problem involved, and someone may wish to argue that such a program may be outside the federal jurisdiction. I doubt if this objection would be seriously raised. The veterans rehabilitation program was designed to give Canadian veterans an opportunity to better fit themselves for return to, or absorption by, the Canadian labour force. This proposed plan would be for exactly the same reason, to take people from the rolls of the unemployed and prepare them for return to and absorption by the Canadian economy. When a person trained in Newfoundland, for example, is able to obtain employment it will relieve, indirectly, the tax burden on every other Canadian from coast to coast. For each person able to obtain employment as a result of such training it would reduce the burden on all the Canadian taxpayers.
I might say, Mr. Chairman, that whether this plan is administered by the federal government or by the provinces is not too important. However, I feel the federal government must take the complete financial responsibility and not load any part of the responsibility on the provinces, and not make the implementation of the plan dependent on additional provincial financial responsibility. I know some of the background as to why it is suggested that the provinces should participate, but I feel the provincial governments already have such a heavy burden that we could not reasonably expect them to participate financially. Particularly would this be true of some of the smaller provinces such as the maritimes, and some of the other provinces which are not as wealthy as the central provinces. I would hope that it could be done completely on

federal initiative. Whether or not it is administered by the federal government is a matter of detail that I would have to leave to the administration.
Notwithstanding the constitution, unemployment is by its very nature and because of its relationship to federal policies particularly federal fiscal and monetary policies, a federal problem, and no federal government can escape its over-all responsibility in this regard. Unemployed people can pass freely from one province to another and they are the concern of all Canadians, and as such should be the concern of this parliament and of this House of Commons. Our labour force must not only be trained but mobile. A pocket of unemployment anywhere in Canada is the concern and responsibility of people in every other part of Canada. I expect the provincial governments would welcome any proposal which would tend to reduce the ranks of the unemployed and to mitigate, whether directly or indirectly, those many economic and social problems connected with unemployment.
I wish to compliment the minister on the increased emphasis he is putting on vocational training. I note the increase in expenditures for vocational training under item 170; but most of this money is being used to train new people who are coming into the labour force, young people who are just making their way into the labour force. A very small proportion of it is being used for the rehabilitation and training of unemployed workers. The increase in this year's estimate specifically on behalf of unemployed workers is very small.
I think modern society accepts the responsibility, though not adequately, for people without jobs. People who are unemployed must not be denied food, clothing and shelter. We have reached a state in our evolution where we believe we are our brothers' keepers at least to the extent that we have to provide them with the basic necessities of life. It would be incredible if we in a great, rich, growing country such as ours could not supply our unemployed people with at least sufficient of the basic requisites of food, clothing and shelter.
Whether these are paid for through unemployment insurance, municipal relief, or through some other means, they are a charge on the community at large and are paid for by the taxpaying and consuming public. We find ourselves, I think, believing that this money comes out of some pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. If we trace it back we find that it all comes from the same source, namely from all of us as workers, from all of us as consumers, and we all have to pay the shot.

The unemployment insurance fund and relief are just two more of those fixed costs which we talk about, costs which raise the prices of our products and make it more difficult for us to compete in world markets. Expenditure for a rehabilitation program- and it would be a considerable expenditure; I do not deny that-would be in the nature of an investment. It would result ultimately in very handsome dividends, not only in the self-respect and dignity of the individuals themselves but to the community at large. This is a program which, though not self-liquidating in the normal terminology of self-liquidating, would be far more than self-liquidating in the ultimate and total effect on the Canadian economy. More important, Mr. Chairman, would be the tens of thousands of individuals who would regain their dignity, self-respect and independent place in the community.
This plan, Mr. Chairman, is complementary to the one put forward yesterday by my leader. These are both partial solutions to a very serious problem. They could be studied. At the same time they could both be discussed with the provinces at a conference such as that suggested yesterday by my leader, the leader of the official opposition.
In conclusion, I would suggest that the government give serious consideration to this proposal. I can assure them that they would receive wholehearted support and backing from members on this side of the house. This is the type of progressive peacetime policy which we as members of parliament and as representatives of the people have an obligation and a responsibility to put forward, and not only just to put forward but to implement.
I suggest with deference to the government that, just as with the proposal for next year's winter works program, they do not leave consideration of this until next fall but that they consider it urgently and immediately, because the days and weeks have a habit of slipping by so quickly that before we know it next winter will be upon us, and only plans which are commenced now can possibly be achieved and implemented by the fall of the year. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, provision could be made in the supplementary estimates which would enable a start to be made and the machinery to be set up. It is obvious that it would not be possible to achieve maximum enrolment at once because of the difficulty of obtaining and perhaps training the teachers, the supervisors, the instructors and other personnel necessary to organize such a large scale enterprise. But once it was started it
Supply-Labour
would grow and would be a permanent and dynamic fixture of our economy in a growing technological age.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I would like to thank the committee for listening so carefully to this proposition. Again on behalf of those on this side of the house I recommend it to the sympathetic consideration of the government, and I can promise that if they would implement this, or some scheme based upon similar lines, they would receive enthusiastic and considerable support from all of us over here.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I represent a riding where workers account for about 50 per cent of the population, I feel I must take part in this debate so as to acquaint the house and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) with the views of the people in my riding as regards unemployment insurance.
But before doing so, Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few words in rebuttal of some arguments advanced in this house, more particularly last night by hon. members for Hull (Mr. Caron), and for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau).
I should like to ask the house to look back on conditions as they were at the time when hon. members of the Liberal party were managing the affairs of this country. They would have us believe that Liberal times were invariably prosperous times, whereas under Conservative administration, Canada lapsed into unrelieved hard times.
If I may, Mr. Chairman, I should hark back to the late twenties, when a Liberal government was sitting on the government benches. Farmers remember, for instance, that butter, at the time, was selling for 18 to 20 cents a pound; eggs, 12 to 15 cents a dozen; hogs $10 to $12; and milk about 80 cents a hundredweight.
On leaving college, I spent a few months looking for work, because it was a period of unemployment, although, it will be noted, this was under a Liberal government. Finally, I found a job that was paying me $6 a week. The facts, therefore, are somewhat different from what hon. members in the opposition would have people believe. But these gentlemen have so taken advantage of the good faith of the public that, sooner or later, they are bound to regret their irresponsible statements.
I also like other citizens of St. Hyacinthe, witnessed practices bordering on inhumanity resorted by the town's mayor, a Liberal. During the depression of the 30's, people were being hired at 10 cents an hour

Supply-Labour
to break up stone with a sledge-hammer. Please note, sir, that this was under a Liberal administration, for it was the Hon. T. D. Bouchard, mayor of St. Hyacinthe, who was responsible for those conditions.
In 1933, the business picture brightened up somewhat. However, at that time, when I was working for the Goodyear Company, men were being paid $6 and $7 a week. This went on until 1939. Now the conditions I have referred to were those that existed during the years 1936, 1937 and 1938, therefore under a Liberal regime. Yet, according to our good friends, whenever they were in power these were years only of prosperity and even of opulence.
I am pointing this out Mr. Chairman, so as to give a complete picture of the conditions then prevailing in Canada. It is easy to brag about prosperity while looking at only one side of the picture, but in these matters, as in any others, it is necessary to look at both sides.
Since the beginning of this session, and especially since the house took up the estimates of the Department of Labour, our Liberal opponents have been painting a very dark picture of the present situation and of unemployment.

In yesterday's edition of La Presse, I found still another headline which might also help write the story of this Conservative government. Indeed, in its issue of yesterday, May 6, La Presse had a heading which read:

for nothing. However, I do not think we have yet reached that stage, and we hope with God's help that present conditions will go on improving as they have done until now.
Meanwhile, our Liberal friends keep on saying that this government has done nothing to alleviate hardships. They are not the only ones who feel sorry for the unemployed. We on this side of the house are concerned with human suffering and are just as anxious as are our opponents

perhaps even more concerned, because we are proving it-to alleviate the regrettable effects that are being felt by these people.
Just to go on with my enumeration, let me also remind the house that it was through the actions of this government that unemployment insurance benefits were granted to fishermen. Following an amendment introduced by the Conservative government, 13,000 fishermen received an amount of about $15 million.
And finally, at the suggestion of the present Minister of Labour, the duration of unemployment insurance benefit payments will soon be extended from 36 to 52 weeks per year.
If you add up all the money spent by this government to help the unemployed, you reach a figure of $68 million. I think our Liberal opponents should at least be realistic and admit that the payment of such an amount certainly deserves the gratitude of the people concerned.
And now, Mr. Chairman, what about the winter works promoted by this government? Such works, amounting to $97,903,000-or almost $98 million-provided employment to close to 40,000 people-39,961, to be exact.
In the province of Quebec, this winter works program reached an amount of $33,450,000 and provided employment for 6,229 persons. I therefore suggest to our Liberal friends to take a good look at the present situation and to represent it in its true light, instead of raising the cry of depression and trying to have everyone, including people in employment, believe that there is a shortage of jobs.
